newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU gears itself for 21st century at summit.
newsitem.headline: EU gears itself for 21st century at summit.

text.p: The European Union was headed confidently towards the 21st century on Sunday after a Dublin summit which laid the foundations for a new economic order and an attack on the ills of drugs, crime and unemployment.

But EU leaders left their weekend get-together knowing the next summit in Amsterdam in June will have to take difficult decisions on how the EU functions when it absorbs a dozen or more new members -- decisions which showed deep divisions at the Dublin talks.
EU leaders said the summit smoothed the way for closer economic integration but heard once again, possibly for the last time, the dissenting voice of British Prime Minister John Major.

Major, facing defeat at a general election due by May, cast doubt about how and if a more integrated EU would work and warned that a two-speed bloc, with stronger states powering ahead, would "blow the EU wide apart."
But Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told the closing news conference that the summit had helped Ireland reach its EU presidency goals of "stable money, more jobs and safer streets".
His satisfaction was echoed by West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl who said: "I hope everyone has now understood that the caravan is moving ahead...that there is no alternative to a united Europe."
Bruton expressed pride in a hard-won accord on a stability pact of strict financial discipline to underpin the single euro currency the bloc hopes to launch by the turn of the century.

It will impose stiff fines on members of economic and monetary union (EMU) if they run up budget deficits in excess of three per cent of gross domestic product in an attempt to make the euro as solid as the deutschemark or Swiss franc.

Bruton said the pact would create a zone of monetary stability from Sicily to Ireland's Western shores - "stable money from Palermo to Clifden" -- and would by itself help cut into the bloc's 18.5 million-strong unemployment queues.

The Irish government also took pride in a concerted attack on the drug menance by agreeing closer cooperation between police and customs against traffickers and organised crime which makes millions from the misery of drug users.
It also rallied EU support for a Dublin Declaration to cut unemployment by coordinating policies to train and adapt the work force for fast-moving free markets.

Major, again the lone voice of opposition, said the declaration would "not create a single job" and said the creation of employment was a national matter on which Britain was teaching the rest of the EU a lesson.

But he reserved his most caustic criticism for the preparation by an intergovernmental conference (IGC) of a new treaty to streamline EU decision making for the time when its west European members are joined by former communist states.

Ireland presented a draft treaty for leaders which they must agree at the Amsterdam summit but glossed over or simply left out the most contentious subjects such as the use of the veto, which some want replaced by qualified majority voting.
"We are not prepared to surrender the veto," said Major.
At issue is how the EU will reach decisions when formal talks to expand its membership begin some six months after the new treaty is agreed.
EU leaders were joined in Dublin by counterparts from Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Romania and Cyprus.
They discussed their membership applications with EU leaders and how Eastern Europe can help fight drugs by cracking down on the growing trade across their borders.
